hero.headline: Port St. Lucie road partially collapses after flooding as neighbor warns of growing hole
hero.body:
A road and nearby property in Port St. Lucie partially collapsed during historic flooding, leaving a hole that a neighbor says has continued to grow each day. The damage developed as floodwater poured into the area and the ground buckled before giving way. Sections of the road and adjoining property fell into the hole, with aerial views showing the extent of the collapse. Yoshi Duran, who lives nearby, pointed out the damage close to her home and described how much of the area had been underwater. “All this was flooded,” she said.

Duran said the widening hole has left her worried about another collapse and what the damage could mean for the homes around it. Her concern is not just about the road that has already fallen away, but also about whether more ground could give way as the hole expands. “It’s not anything to laugh about. It is a dangerous situation because they’re not knowing when it can cave in,” Duran said. She said the hole has grown daily since the flooding. As she watches the damage spread, she is pressing the city for answers about the situation near her home.

City public information officer Scott Samples said excess water on the road and in a culvert beneath it caused the damage. Officials are aware of the collapse and are assessing how best to repair it. Samples said the city wants to move quickly, but determining the right approach takes time. “We want to repair these as quickly as we possibly can. Unfortunately, it takes some time,” he said. The city is still working out how to address the damaged area, and Samples said studies may be necessary before crews can begin the repair work. Samples said the city’s goal is to make sure the work is done properly, even if that requires further evaluation before construction starts. “You want to make sure you’re doing it as well and as correctly as you possibly can. So that may require some studies to take place before you actually start the work,” he said. For Duran, the continuing growth of the hole makes answers urgent. “We understand everybody is short-staffed. But we need answers,” she said.

hero.headline: Flood watch canceled for Indian River County; road and school closures remain
hero.body:
The National Weather Service canceled the flood watch for Indian River County Friday morning, while flooding and roadway damage continued to affect travel and the School District of Indian River County remained closed Friday.

Additional showers remain possible, but the heaviest rainfall threat is farther north, according to Indian River County Emergency Services. Officials urged drivers to check road conditions before traveling, allow extra time for detours and never drive through flooded roads.

The county identified these locations among those affected by flooding or roadway damage Friday:

• U.S. 1 near Barber Street: Partial blockage.
• Old Dixie Highway SW: Flooding and partial blockages at several locations.
• 82nd Avenue at the entrance to Heritage Plantation: Partial blockage.
• Skyline Drive, from Periwinkle to Barber Street: Partial blockage.
• 130th Street: Closed.
• 79th Street west of 130th Avenue: Closed because of a roadway washout.
• 13th Street SW east of 66th Avenue SW: Closed because of roadway damage.
• Vero Lake Estates: 104th Avenue between 87th and 93rd streets, and 83rd Street between 91st and 93rd avenues, are closed.

Drivers can check the county’s live road closure map for additional closures and updates. Officials said water needs time to recede, and damaged roads must be assessed and repaired before they can safely reopen. Crews are working in affected areas, and drivers are asked to give them room and follow barricades.

Marian Fell Library and the Veterans Services office in Sebastian remain closed. The Indian River County Shooting Range, Gifford Aquatic Center and North County Aquatic Center are open Friday. Families can check the School District of Indian River County website for updates on the district closure.

The county said the Indian River County Fairgrounds may be used in the coming days to support emergency management missions for communities to the north, where the threat of heavy rain and flooding is greater.

hero.headline: Martin County cancels Kanner Highway data center meeting, promises public forums
hero.body:
Martin County canceled a Friday staff meeting about a proposed data center off Kanner Highway, citing overwhelming public interest, and promised future public meetings and workshops. Residents gathered outside the Martin County Administrative Center anyway, demanding answers about the development west of Interstate 95, roughly half a mile from Crystal Lake Elementary School. The project remains under review and could qualify for administrative approval without a public hearing or a recorded vote by county commissioners.

The county announced the cancellation Thursday evening, less than 17 hours before the meeting was scheduled to begin. Deputy Growth Management Director Pete Walden said members of the public had requested the informal question-and-answer session with Growth Management Department staff. He said it was intended for questions, rather than a decision on the application, but information circulating online created the impression that officials were privately considering approval. Interest eventually exceeded the county’s capacity to accommodate attendees, he said. “We could not accommodate that. We didn't have any rooms or anything available for that size,” Walden said.

The potential approval process is another focus of residents’ objections. A county ordinance adopted in 2010 established administrative approval for certain targeted industries to encourage economic development. Data centers fall within those classifications. Walden said an existing planned unit development agreement also covers the proposal and allows qualifying targeted industries on platted industrial lots to receive administrative approval. Commissioners approved a one-year moratorium on data centers Oct. 27 while the county reviews its development regulations. County officials said this application was submitted before the moratorium was proposed, making the project exempt from that temporary restriction.

Residents raised concerns about potential noise from cooling equipment, water consumption, electricity demand, higher utility bills, wildlife displacement, property values and possible health effects on children at Crystal Lake Elementary School. Those concerns are questions about potential impacts, rather than established consequences of the development. Chris McIntyre, whose son graduated from the school, was among those seeking answers Friday. “We need answers, and we need them quick,” he said. Dan Wilson, president of the Locks Landing homeowners association, represents a community less than two miles from the proposed site.

Walden said the county will review potential impacts before deciding whether to approve the project. A staff report examining the application is expected in December. After that report, county officials plan a public forum where residents can ask questions and learn more about the development, likely including a presentation from the applicant.
hero.article_text: A controversial proposal to build a more than 5.7 million-square-foot data center just half a mile from an elementary school is drawing growing opposition in Martin County, where residents are raising concerns about everything from environmental impacts to whether they'll have a say in the project's approval.WATCH: 'We need answers': Martin Co. officials address outrage over proposed data centerOn Friday morning, a small but vocal group of residents gathered outside the Martin County Administrative Center, demanding answers about the massive development proposed for a parcel of land off Kanner Highway, west of Interstate 95.They had planned to attend a meeting with the county's Growth Management Department. But less than 17 hours before it was scheduled to begin, the county canceled it, citing overwhelming public interest.Residents showed up anyway."We need answers, and we need them quick," said Chris McIntyre, whose son graduated from nearby Crystal Lake Elementary School. "This story cannot die, or else this is the death of Crystal Lake School."McIntyre, who goes by Coach Mack, became emotional discussing what the proposed development could mean for the school and surrounding neighborhoods."Now that's the death of an A-rated elementary school that I love," he said, his voice breaking.He's far from alone.Residents have raised concerns about potential noise pollution, water consumption, increased electricity demand, higher utility bills, wildlife displacement, declining property values and possible health impacts on children attending Crystal Lake Elementary.Michael Panella, another resident opposing the project, became emotional while explaining why the fight is so personal."It's life. These little ones are innocent," Panella said, referring also to students of Crystal Lake. Dan Wilson, president of the Locks Landing homeowners association, represents a community less than two miles from the proposed site.“They’re probably dropping now because, oh, the data center going there. We don’t want to move there,” Wilson said of property values."We have residences right here, tons of residents. We're all going to have to deal with this."Residents acknowledge they don't yet know for sure what the long-term consequences of the project might be. They don't know whether electricity bills will increase, how much noise the facility could generate or what wildlife habitat might be lost.But they do know that once something of this magnitude is built, there's no easy way to undo it.The controversy intensified Thursday evening when Martin County announced the cancellation of an informal Growth Management meeting scheduled for 9:30 a.m. 19, the Martin County Board of County Commissioners posted the following message online:For residents who had planned to attend, the cancellation only added to their frustration."The thing that frustrates me the most about this is the fact that they were willing to do this meeting in private," said resident Alisha Gibbs.Gibbs described herself as "disgusted" and "absolutely appalled" by the situation.But Martin County Deputy Growth Management Director Pete Walden told WPTV Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey that the meeting was never intended to be a formal public hearing or a decision-making session.Instead, Walden said, it was an informal meeting requested by members of the public who wanted to ask county staff questions about the development — something his department routinely accommodates for other projects.He said information about the meeting circulated online, creating the impression that county officials were privately considering a decision on the data center.When interest grew beyond what the county could accommodate, officials decided to cancel."We could not accommodate that. We didn't have any rooms or anything available for that size," Walden explained. "So we had to cancel, and we'll do some workshops in the future. I believe the applicant is also going to reach out for some public presentations on the subject." When asked why residents weren't being given more opportunities to weigh in, Walden maintained the county has been transparent."We are transparent through the process, and everything can be made available to anyone that is interested," he said.Walden said additional public meetings and workshops will be scheduled to allow residents to ask questions and learn more about the project.But the canceled meeting is only one of several controversies surrounding the development.Another major point of contention is the timing of the developer's application.On Oct. 27, Martin County commissioners approved a one-year moratorium on data centers, temporarily restricting new applications while the county reviews its development regulations.But records show the application for this project was submitted the day before the moratorium was proposed on October 13. That timing means the project is not subject to the temporary restriction, according to county officials.Walden acknowledged the timing but said the county cannot control when developers submit applications."They obviously saw like everybody else that a moratorium was coming, and they got their application in ahead of time," Walden said. "We don't direct applicants ... and we certainly can't pick and choose when these things happen."WPTV reached out to the project applicant and the law firm representing it, requesting comment on the timing of the application and residents' environmental, energy and health concerns.Neither responded by publication time.Perhaps the most significant concern for opponents is whether residents will have any formal say in the project's approval.Under a county ordinance adopted in 2010, during the Great Recession, Martin County established an administrative approval process for certain targeted industries to encourage economic development.Data centers fall within the county's targeted industry classifications. According to Walden, the proposed development is also covered by an existing planned unit development, or PUD, agreement that allows qualifying targeted industries on platted industrial lots to receive administrative approval.That means the project could potentially move forward without a public hearing or recorded vote by county commissioners.For residents demanding a voice in the decision, that distinction is critical.Hussey asked Walden whether there was anything the county could do to give residents more of a say in whether the development is approved."With the moratorium, we'll be looking at our code to make revisions so everything is appropriately reviewed as it comes in," Walden said."To give the public more of a say in future projects?" Hussey asked. "Correct," Walden responded. Residents are also demanding answers about how a development of this size could affect surrounding neighborhoods, wildlife and students at Crystal Lake Elementary School.The proposal initially called for just under 1 million square feet of development. hero.headline: Martin County cancels data-center meeting; project could advance without commission vote
hero.body:
Martin County canceled an informal meeting about a proposed data center amid growing public interest, while officials said the project could receive administrative approval without a public hearing or county commission vote. Residents gathered Friday morning outside the Martin County Administrative Center despite the cancellation announced Thursday evening. The proposed development is off Kanner Highway, west of Interstate 95, about half a mile from Crystal Lake Elementary School. Deputy Growth Management Director Pete Walden said the project has not been approved and will undergo staff review before any approval decision.

Walden said the Growth Management Department meeting was requested by residents seeking answers from county staff, rather than arranged as a formal hearing or decision-making session. As information circulated online, interest grew beyond what the county could accommodate, he said. The county expects to release a staff report examining the project in December, then schedule a public forum where residents can ask questions. Officials anticipate that forum will include a presentation from the applicant. “This is our first data center to be reviewed. We're going to take our time ... and make sure everything is properly vetted,” Walden said.

The potential administrative approval stems from a county ordinance adopted in 2010 to encourage economic development through certain targeted industries, including data centers. Walden said an existing planned unit development agreement also allows qualifying targeted industries on platted industrial lots to receive administrative approval. County commissioners approved a one-year moratorium on data centers Oct. 27 while the county reviews its development regulations. County officials said this application predates the moratorium proposal and is exempt from the temporary restriction. Walden said the county will examine code revisions intended to give the public more input on future projects.

Residents opposing the development raised concerns about potential noise from cooling equipment, water consumption, electricity demand, higher utility bills, wildlife displacement, property values and children's health. Those are concerns about possible effects, rather than established impacts of this proposal. Dan Wilson, president of the Locks Landing homeowners association, represents a community less than two miles from the site. Chris McIntyre, whose son graduated from Crystal Lake Elementary School, called for quick answers. Resident Alisha Gibbs criticized the canceled meeting and called for the county to reject the project. Walden said staff will review potential impacts before deciding whether to approve it.

hero.headline: Flood watch canceled for Indian River County; roads and schools remain closed
hero.body:
The National Weather Service canceled a Flood Watch for Indian River County Friday morning, but flooded and damaged roads remain closed across the county, and the School District of Indian River County is closed Friday.

Additional showers remain possible, though the heaviest rainfall threat is farther north, according to Indian River County Emergency Services. Officials are asking drivers to check road conditions before traveling, allow extra time for detours and never drive through flooded roads.

Flooding or roadway damage was affecting these locations Friday:

• U.S. 1 near Barber Street: Partial blockage.
• Old Dixie Highway SW: Flooding and partial blockages at several locations.
• 82nd Avenue at the entrance to Heritage Plantation: Partial blockage.
• Skyline Drive, from Periwinkle to Barber Street: Partial blockage.
• 130th Street: Closed.
• 79th Street west of 130th Avenue: Closed because of a roadway washout.
• 13th Street SW east of 66th Avenue SW: Closed because of roadway damage.
• Vero Lake Estates: 104th Avenue between 87th and 93rd streets, and 83rd Street between 91st and 93rd avenues, are closed.

The county said the list covers selected locations. Drivers can check the county’s live road closure map for additional closures and updates. Water needs time to recede, and damaged roads must be assessed and repaired before they can safely reopen, officials said. Crews are working in affected areas, and drivers are asked to give them room and follow barricades.

The Indian River County Shooting Range, Gifford Aquatic Center and North County Aquatic Center are open Friday. Marian Fell Library and the Veterans Services office in Sebastian remain closed. School district updates are available on the district website.

The county said the Indian River County Fairgrounds may be used in the coming days to support emergency management missions for communities to the north, where the threat of heavy rain and flooding is greater.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie extends boil water notice for about 21,000 customers in Tradition, west areas
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie has extended a precautionary boil water notice affecting about 21,000 customers in Tradition and western neighborhoods after Tuesday's water main break near Glades Cut Off Road. Water quality testing remains underway, and city officials said the notice will stay in place until testing is successfully completed and the city determines it is safe to lift.

The notice covers all of Tradition, including Western Grove, Riverland, Wilson Grove and Southern Grove, as well as areas west of Interstate 95 south to Becker Road. Communities along Glades Cut Off Road, including Copper Creek, Wylder and Verano, are also affected.

City officials said the number of affected customers requires a significant number of water samples to be collected and tested to ensure the water is safe. The city is asking residents not to tamper with clearly marked hydrants or pipes that are flushing water. Interference could delay testing and extend the notice, officials warned.

According to city officials, a contractor working on a construction project unrelated to the city damaged the 36-inch water main. Crews responded and repaired the main within hours, then began the required flushing process.

The city is investigating the incident and expects to pursue appropriate action to recover costs from those responsible. Residents can find updates at CityofPSL.com.

hero.headline: Flooding closes about 12 roads in Indian River County, limits Vero Lake Estates access
hero.body:
About 12 roads were closed in Indian River County Thursday evening as renewed flooding restricted access in Vero Lake Estates. The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office urged drivers to avoid unnecessary travel and stay off flooded roads as water continued to affect neighborhoods.

Indian River County Public Schools will be closed Friday because of the flooding. The latest high water comes just weeks after another round of flooding affected parts of the Treasure Coast. County officials reported multiple road closures in Vero Lake Estates, where water surrounding parts of the neighborhood left some residents with limited ways to get around.

Terry Holly, who moved to the area from Pennsylvania with his wife 23 years ago, said his household had supplies to manage the disruption. “We’re stuck another week. Luckily, we’ve got plenty of groceries and water, so we’re all set,” Holly said. He said he and other residents had dropped their flood insurance policies, but repeated flooding has him reconsidering. “We all dropped it. And we haven’t had it since, but now I’m going to rethink it again,” he said.

Holly warned that smaller vehicles could struggle to travel through the standing water. “The trucks and the high vehicles can get through. The small cars, forget it,” he said. Fellow resident Marjorie Hale also raised concerns about traffic, particularly drivers moving too quickly through flooded neighborhoods and the waves their vehicles send toward nearby homes. She said older properties were a particular concern.

Hale said she believes this round of flooding has been handled better than the previous one, with more precautions being taken. Her neighborhood flooded during the earlier round, too. She urged drivers to slow down and consider the people living along flooded streets.

For some families, Friday’s school closure means an early start to Thanksgiving break. Hale said her daughter is old enough to stay home while she works. With other families across the Treasure Coast dealing with more serious flooding and damage to their homes, Hale encouraged neighbors to help one another. “Invite your neighbors to Thanksgiving,” she said.

cards.headline: Vero Beach sets daily rainfall record at 2.25 inches; drier weather expected Sunday
cards.teaser: Thursday’s rainfall topped Vero Beach’s previous daily record of 1.73 inches, set in 1987. A few showers could linger into the weekend before drier weather begins Sunday.
cards.body:
Vero Beach recorded 2.25 inches of rain Thursday, breaking the city’s previous daily rainfall record of 1.73 inches set in 1987. Heavy rain also set a daily record in West Palm Beach, where 3.08 inches fell, surpassing the previous record of 2.99 inches set in 2021. The record-setting totals followed rounds of rain across parts of South Florida and the Treasure Coast. The wet weather has eased, but a few lingering showers remain possible heading into the weekend.

Friday’s forecast calls for cloudy conditions and temperatures near normal for this time of year, with highs in the upper 70s and low 80s. Some areas could have fog during the morning hours. Rain chances remain low, although a stray shower cannot be ruled out.

Saturday is expected to bring a mix of sun and clouds, with temperatures reaching the low 80s. Isolated showers are possible during the afternoon, with rain chances around 30%.

Drier weather is forecast to begin Sunday, and most of next week is expected to stay dry. A cold front approaching Wednesday could bring a few showers. The front is also expected to cool temperatures into the mid-70s by Thanksgiving.

hero.headline: Hobe Sound singer steps in for duet with Matthew Morrison at Maltz Jupiter Theatre
hero.body:
Hobe Sound singer Emily Rynasko joined Broadway and “Glee” star Matthew Morrison for a duet at Maltz Jupiter Theatre after an FAA ground stop prevented much of his ensemble from arriving. Morrison texted Rynasko to ask her to sing with him, giving her only hours to prepare for the performance.

“I found out about 9:30 in the morning, and the show was at 7:30 that night,” Rynasko said. She had watched “Glee” when she was younger and said she never expected an invitation from the actor who played William Schuester. Together, they sang “Somewhere Over the Rainbow.”

Rynasko grew up in Hobe Sound and began her musical training as a child at Maltz Jupiter Theatre. She credited that training, including sight-reading and using her ear, with preparing her to take on the short-notice performance. “It’s being a trained musician that’s part of your job,” Rynasko said. Returning to the theater also meant performing at a place she considers home and among people she considers family.

“I was a lot calmer than I thought I would be because I treated it like any other show that I had done,” Rynasko said. She also spoke about honoring the teachers, community, friends and family who have been part of her journey. “That’s what brings me joy and carries me through.”

hero.headline: Indian River County public schools to close Friday, Nov. 20, amid flooding
hero.body:
All public schools in Indian River County will be closed Friday, Nov. 20, as flooding, waterlogged ground and the chance of additional heavy rain raise safety concerns. The School District of Indian River County announced the closure Thursday, saying it was taking the step to protect students, their families and district employees. The decision comes as roads across parts of the county are closed and water levels are rising at a district transportation facility. The district pointed to a growing number of road closures, especially in Vero Lake Estates, among the conditions behind its decision to keep schools closed Friday.

Flooding also is affecting the district’s North County Transportation compound, where officials reported rising water. Across the county, the road closure map showed nine road closures and four lane closures Thursday. The roads listed as closed included 100th Court, 103rd Avenue, 104th Avenue, 83rd Street and 87th Street. Those five roads were among the closures shown on the map, rather than the full list of affected roads. The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office also reported additional flooded roads in Vero Lake Estates, the same community the school district highlighted when explaining the closure.

The Sheriff’s Office urged drivers to stay out of standing water. Water covering a road can be deeper than it looks, and vehicles can stall if drivers attempt to pass through it. The warning applies to flooded stretches even when a driver cannot easily judge the depth of the water ahead. High-water vehicles are in the area, according to the Sheriff’s Office. Anyone who becomes stranded should call 911. The safety warning comes alongside the reports of more flooded roads in Vero Lake Estates and the road and lane closures listed on the county’s map Thursday.

A flood watch remains in place for Indian River County through Friday evening, with more showers and thunderstorms possible. The National Weather Service reported that parts of eastern Indian River County had received 2 to 4 inches of rain. The possibility of more heavy rain, combined with ground already saturated and localized flooding, was part of the district’s explanation for closing schools. Friday’s closure applies to all of the county’s public schools. Schools also will be closed for Thanksgiving break. For Friday, the district said its decision centers on the safety of students, families and employees amid the flooding and road closures.

cards.headline: Indian River County extends emergency through Nov. 23 as more flooding threatens
cards.teaser: The county reported two properties destroyed and seven with major damage from the previous storm. Officials warn that saturated ground could leave additional areas vulnerable to flooding.
cards.body:
Indian River County has extended its local state of emergency through Monday, Nov. 23, as officials prepare for more rain and possible flooding in communities already hit by recent storms. As of Tuesday, the county reported two properties destroyed and seven with major damage from the previous storm.

Another 65 properties had minor damage, and 97 others were affected. Earlier this month, flooding left neighborhoods inundated, roads impassable and traffic disrupted. Emergency management officials said the ground is saturated, raising the possibility that additional heavy rain could flood areas that did not flood during the last storm. Officials are closely monitoring Heritage Plantation, Whispering Palms and areas near Highland Drive.

Ryan Lloyd, Deputy Director and Emergency Management Chief for the Indian River County Department of Emergency Services, urged residents throughout the county to prepare for possible flooding. “There could be areas that flood that we're not expecting per se or that necessarily flooded in the past,” Lloyd said. Crews have been cleaning swales and inspecting drainage systems across the county as officials prepare for more rain.

Lloyd also asked residents to avoid driving through flooded neighborhoods simply to look at the damage. “It can create waves that actually go into the houses, and it can make the flooding even worse for residents.” The county's emergency information center is open for questions about the flood threat. Residents can call 772-226-4000 for assistance.

cards.teaser: The junior wide receiver topped 100 total yards in last week's victory and is working toward a state title after Vero Beach reached the championship game in 2025.
cards.body:
Vero Beach High School junior wide receiver Latravious Woods recorded more than 100 total yards and two touchdowns in last week's playoff win over Fort Pierce Central, helping the Fighting Indians continue their pursuit of a state championship.

Woods has reached the playoffs in all three of his high school seasons, including Vero Beach's run to the state championship game in 2025. He grew up watching the Fighting Indians from the stands and joined the team as a freshman. Now a key playmaker and leader, he wants to help Vero Beach finish with a title while keeping his focus on one game at a time.

Fighting Indians Head Coach Lenny Jankowski values Woods' ability to contribute in different roles. "He's a guy that you hope to get the ball in his hands, however it needs to happen," Jankowski said. "And he's got some position versatility."

Woods also emphasizes his effort on plays when the ball goes to a teammate. "Even though I don't have the ball in my hands, I just got to go 100% every play because, you know, if I was to have the ball in my hand, I would want somebody to go 100% for me," Woods said. "So I'm going to give 100% for my teammates and my coaches because I want the same when I have the ball."

As a leader, Woods works to keep teammates encouraged and focused on the coaches' expectations. Returning to the championship game and winning it remains his goal. "Being back there this year and just finishing it all the way this time, it would feel so great," Woods said. "And I know the whole Vero community would love it."

hero.headline: Advocate says warnings preceded St. Lucie County’s historic flooding
hero.body:
St. Lucie County resident and water-policy advocate Nyla Pipes said warnings about flooding risks had been raised weeks before the county’s historic early-November flooding, with other concerns stretching back years. Speaking at a South Florida Water Management District board meeting after the flooding, Pipes challenged the idea that the danger had arrived without warning. The flooding damaged hundreds of homes after more than three days of rain dropped over a foot of water on parts of the county, with some locations recording as much as 17 inches. More heavy rain this week has renewed concerns about the drainage system’s capacity. Schools were closed Wednesday.

Responsibility for drainage is divided among the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, the water management district, the county, cities, local water-control districts and homeowners’ associations. Which agency handles a problem depends on the canal or drainage system involved. Water typically travels through ditches and canals toward the St. Lucie River and Indian River Lagoon before reaching the ocean. During the flooding, unusually high tides restricted that flow. County Commissioner Cathy Townsend said residents called as water rose, asking what officials were doing. She said she could tell them only that floodgates were open and water was moving, despite the worsening conditions.

At the district meeting, board member Thomas Hurley described the flooding as a warning that infrastructure maintenance is becoming more important as water levels rise. Fellow board member Jay Steinle said shortcomings in forecasting equipment had left the district without enough advance notice to lower canal levels and prepare. Pipes, however, said concerns had already been raised. Townsend has called for better maintenance of county canals and ditches and criticized the district’s timing in opening a canal. She said she later learned that an environmental concern had caused the delay. Townsend also acknowledged that earlier openings might not have prevented flooding, given the amount of water the system faced.

The damage revealed weaknesses in newer planned developments, including Tradition. In its Vitalia neighborhood, floodwater submerged streets, stranded vehicles and left some residents without electricity for days. Tradition was built using the existing canal network, and developers were not required to construct a new canal, a possible factor in the community’s drainage problems. The flooding also created financial concerns for homeowners. Many affected properties were outside areas FEMA designates as having a high flood risk, where flood insurance is generally required for federally backed mortgages. Some owners outside those zones may not have carried flood coverage to help pay for repairs.

I happened to know that those alarm bells had sounded some weeks before, but many for the past several years, she said.

hero.headline: Volunteers remove flood-damaged drywall from Jensen Beach's Skyline Drive homes
hero.body:
Volunteers removed flood-damaged drywall Thursday from homes in Jensen Beach's Skyline Drive neighborhood, with demolition and cleanup targeted for completion Saturday. Project LIFT and community partners arrived Thursday morning, two weeks after flooding damaged homes in the neighborhood. Some families are staying with friends or in hotels as Thanksgiving approaches, said Stephen Leighton, the volunteer coordinator with 25 United Disaster Relief.

Leighton said 17 homes in the community sustained water damage. County inspectors are helping homeowners understand the repairs and permits they need. Volunteers working with 25 United carried damaged drywall out of homes and into dumpsters, which are quickly filling as cleanup continues. “So, Project LIFT, working with 25 United, came in, took all the drywall off the walls, took it outside to the dumpster,” Leighton said. Waterlines remained visible on the exposed studs.

Susan Destafney's home is completely gutted, and water damage has left her unable to live there. “We have a long way to go until we rebuild, you know. We’ve demoed, and we’ve got a long future ahead of us, and I know that God will be there for us and everything is going to be good,” Destafney said. Mark Burner, who has lived in the neighborhood for 40 years, expressed gratitude for the volunteers helping residents recover.

Bob Zaccheo, CEO of Project LIFT, emphasized the rebuilding work beyond demolition. “To see these houses getting repaired and torn apart, torn down, is one thing, but built back is a whole other,” Zaccheo said. Leighton said the efforts are being coordinated with state and federal representatives, with the goal of finishing demolition and cleanup by Saturday.

And one local singer can attest.Emily Rynasko, who said she watched "Glee" when she was younger, said she would have never expected a text from the actor who played William Schuester, asking her to sing a duet with him on stage."I found out about 9:30 in the morning, and the show was at 7:30 that night," Emily Rynasko said.It was a moment Rynasko had been working toward her whole life."Learning sight-reading music and just using my ear. It's being a trained musician that's part of your job," Rynasko said.Rynasko, who grew up in Hobe Sound, started that training as a kid at the Maltz Jupiter Theatre."They raised me. The Maltz Jupiter Theater is my, my home, and that is truly my family. They have made me the woman I am," Rynasko said.So when Rynasko stepped into the spotlight to sing Somewhere Over the Rainbow, she treated it like a professional and felt right at home next to Morrison."I was a lot calmer than I thought I would be because I treated it like any other show that I had done," Rynasko said.After all, there's no place like home."To also honor everyone that has been part of your journey, whether it's been a teacher, your community, your friends and family," Rynasko said. "That's what brings me joy and carries me through."This story was reported on-air by journalist Jamie Ostroff and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. hero.headline: Woods scores twice in Vero Beach's playoff win over Fort Pierce Central
hero.body:
Vero Beach High School junior Latravious Woods totaled more than 100 yards and scored two touchdowns in last week's playoff victory over Fort Pierce Central, helping the Fighting Indians continue their push for a state title. The wide receiver has played in the postseason in each of his three high school seasons and was part of Vero Beach's run to the state championship game in 2025. Now, he hopes to help the team return to that stage and win the title, while concentrating on the next game rather than looking too far ahead.

Woods grew up watching the Fighting Indians from the stands before joining the team as a freshman. Since then, he has developed into a player his coaches and teammates rely on, with responsibilities that extend beyond catching passes. Vero Beach head coach Lenny Jankowski said Woods gives the team options in how it uses him. "He's a guy that you hope to get the ball in his hands, however it needs to happen," Jankowski said. "And he's got some position versatility." His production against Fort Pierce Central added another strong performance to his role in the offense during Vero Beach's playoff pursuit.

Woods also takes responsibility for helping teammates understand the program's expectations and keeping their spirits up. "I know a lot about the program and how things and how coaches want things done," Woods said. "I just make sure everybody's just up-notch and like we all on the same level. Nobody heads down." That approach carries into his effort on plays designed for someone else. "Even though I don't have the ball in my hands, I just got to go 100% every play because, you know, if I was to have the ball in my hand, I would want somebody to go 100% for me," he said.

For Woods, giving that effort is a way to support the people around him, not just improve his own numbers. "So I'm going to give 100% for my teammates and my coaches because I want the same when I have the ball," he said. After experiencing a state championship appearance, Woods wants to finish the next trip with a title for the team he once watched as a child. "Being back there this year and just finishing it all the way this time, it would feel so great," Woods said. "And I know the whole Vero community would love it."

hero.headline: Indian River County schools closed Friday, Nov. 20, because of flooding
hero.body:
All schools in the School District of Indian River County will be closed Friday, Nov. 20, because of localized flooding, saturated ground and the potential for additional heavy rain. The district announced the closure Thursday afternoon as road closures increased, particularly in Vero Lake Estates.

Rising water at the North County Transportation compound has also forced the district to move school buses. Schools will remain closed next week for Thanksgiving break, Nov. 23-27. The district said schools are scheduled to reopen Monday, Nov. 30.

cards.headline: Indian River County remains under Flood Watch as more heavy rain threatens
cards.teaser: Road closures and standing water have affected Vero Lake Estates and other parts of Indian River County. Emergency officials urge residents to avoid unnecessary travel as additional rain could worsen flooding.
cards.body:
Indian River County remains under a Flood Watch as additional heavy rain through Saturday threatens areas already saturated by recent rainfall, the National Weather Service said Thursday. With roads affected by closures or standing water, county emergency officials urged residents to stay home unless they need to travel.

The National Weather Service office in Melbourne forecasts a 40% to 60% chance of 3 to 6 inches of additional rain along the east-central Florida coast through Saturday. Saturated soil has made many areas more prone to flooding. If the most likely rainfall totals materialize, scattered pockets of flooding could develop along the coast. The forecast also puts the chance of higher-end totals of 8 to 10 inches or more at 10% in some locations. Those amounts would bring a risk of impactful flash flooding.

Multiple roads in the Vero Lake Estates area and elsewhere in Indian River County have had closures or standing water this week because of the saturated ground. The Indian River County Emergency Operations Center continues to monitor weather and road conditions. It warned that floodwater and road damage can be difficult to see after dark.

Residents should check the county’s road closure map before traveling and never drive through flooded roads or around barricades, emergency officials said. A road may be unsafe even if the map does not show it as closed.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County schools to close Friday as heavy rain threatens morning commute
hero.body:
St. Lucie County schools will be closed Friday, Nov. 20, as additional heavy rain threatens the morning trip to school in already saturated areas, district officials announced Thursday. The district said it made the decision out of caution because the heaviest rainfall could coincide with the arrival of students and staff.

After a break in the rain Thursday afternoon, the National Weather Service is forecasting another 3 to 4 inches or more overnight and into Friday morning, according to the district. The heaviest rain is expected around the time students and staff would normally travel to school. District officials cited student and staff safety, along with saturated conditions throughout the community, as the reasons for closing schools.

All after-school programs scheduled for Friday are canceled, including aftercare, activities and athletic events. The closure means students will begin their Thanksgiving holiday early. Students are scheduled to return to school Monday, Nov. 30.

District officials will decide later Friday whether the SAT scheduled for Saturday, Nov. 21, will take place. The district said it will communicate that decision to families as soon as possible.

hero.headline: Deputies seek missing 15-year-old last seen running toward Jonathan Dickinson State Park
hero.body:
The Martin County Sheriff’s Office is asking for the public’s help finding Stephen Levi Cotela, 15, who was last seen running north toward Jonathan Dickinson State Park. His last known location was near SE County Line Road and SE Harken Terrace in Tequesta.

Cotela has been missing since 3:30 p.m., according to the Sheriff’s Office. Deputies said he got out of his father’s vehicle after an argument and ran toward the park.

Cotela is 5 feet 5 inches tall, weighs approximately 120 to 130 pounds and has black hair and brown eyes. He was last seen wearing a gray t-shirt, black sweatpants and sandals.

cards.headline: Martin County School Board reinstates Matthew Theobald, awards back pay
cards.teaser: The board rescinded the Spectrum Academy teacher’s suspension and termination after a judge ruled his comments about Charlie Kirk’s death did not justify dismissal.
cards.body:
The Martin County School Board voted this week to reinstate Spectrum Academy teacher Matthew Theobald and rescind his suspension and termination after adopting a judge’s recommendation. The judge had ruled that Theobald’s social media comments about conservative activist Charlie Kirk’s death did not justify suspension or dismissal. Theobald will also be awarded back pay and benefits through June 30.

The Martin County School District sought to dismiss Theobald over several online comments following Kirk’s murder in Utah in September 2025. The school board voted to suspend Theobald without pay and recommended his termination. Both parties agreed to an administrative hearing to address the matter.

In June, the judge ruled that the school board failed to prove Theobald engaged in immorality or willful neglect of duty, which would have been grounds for dismissal. The judge also found that Theobald’s Facebook comments did not disrupt his students or the learning environment, or reduce any teacher’s ability to teach. District leadership said after the ruling that it would review the recommendation.

School board member Marsha Powers said she voted in favor of the decision but questioned the process. “I have serious concerns about the process that brought this matter before a judge who does not live or work in the community,” Powers said.

Board member Tony Anderson said he understood Powers’ concerns but noted that the board had already placed the issue in the judge’s hands. “It’s a decision we have to live with,” Anderson said.

hero.headline: TRICARE authorizes emergency prescription refills in Florida through Nov. 29
hero.body:
The Defense Health Agency has authorized temporary emergency prescription refills through Nov. 29 for TRICARE beneficiaries in flood-affected Florida counties, including Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River. Beneficiaries needing a refill should take their prescription bottle to any TRICARE retail network pharmacy.

If the bottle is unavailable or its label is damaged or missing, beneficiaries should contact Express Scripts or a retail network pharmacy for assistance. To find a network pharmacy, beneficiaries can call Express Scripts at 1-877-363-1303.

When possible, beneficiaries should use the pharmacy where their prescription was originally filled, according to the agency. A prescription filled by a retail chain may also be filled at another location operated by that chain. Beneficiaries whose prescribing clinician is available can ask the clinician to call a new prescription into a network pharmacy.

The waiver applies to counties affected by fall flooding. It also covers Brevard, Broward, DeSoto, Duval, Flagler, Glades, Hardee, Hendry, Highlands, Miami-Dade, Monroe, Okeechobee, Palm Beach, Putnam, Seminole and Volusia counties.

TRICARE beneficiaries other than active-duty service members may also receive urgent care from any TRICARE-authorized urgent care center or provider without a referral, according to the Defense Health Agency. That option allows beneficiaries to seek nonemergency treatment when their primary care provider is unavailable because of an emergency.

Anyone who reasonably believes they are experiencing a medical emergency should call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room.

hero.headline: 18-year-old arrested in Port St. Lucie hit-and-run that critically injured scooter rider
hero.body:
An 18-year-old driver has been arrested on a felony charge of leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury after a woman riding an electric scooter to work was struck in Port St. Lucie, police said. The Port St. Lucie Police Department identified the driver as Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer. Investigators say he struck the 24-year-old woman and left the scene of Monday morning’s crash near Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace.

The woman was traveling west on the sidewalk toward Southwest Rosser Boulevard and had entered a crosswalk when a gray Chevrolet Tahoe making a left turn onto Southwest Feather Terrace hit her, investigators said. Police said she was wearing a helmet. Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said Tuesday that she remained unconscious and in critical condition. “We’re deeply concerned for her recovery, and our thoughts are with her loved ones,” Niemczyk said. A witness stopped to help the woman, called 911 and obtained the SUV’s license plate information. Investigators used that information to identify the vehicle and driver, police said.

Sanchez-Chasmer had two friends with him and had been playing a “ding-dong-ditch” prank shortly before the crash, investigators said. Niemczyk said they had been at a house belonging to a friend and fled when the friend’s mother came to the door. Investigators believe the people inside the SUV realized a collision had occurred, according to Niemczyk. He said Sanchez-Chasmer and the two passengers left without calling 911.

Niemczyk said the decision to leave the scene was central to the criminal investigation. “Had they remained on scene, provided aid, it would have been a very different criminal outcome,” he said. “There probably wouldn’t have been criminal charges at that point.” The investigation remains active, and toxicology results are pending, according to police.

hero.headline: Indian River County schools closed Friday, Nov. 20, due to flooding, rain threat
hero.body:
All schools in the School District of Indian River County will be closed Friday, Nov. 20, because of localized flooding, saturated ground and the potential for additional heavy rain, the district announced Thursday afternoon.

The district cited increasing road closures, particularly in Vero Lake Estates. Rising water at the North County Transportation compound has also forced the district to move school buses.

Schools will remain closed next week for Thanksgiving break, Nov. 23-27. The district said schools are scheduled to reopen Monday, Nov. 30.

cards.headline: Indian River County extends emergency through Nov. 23 amid renewed flood threat
cards.teaser: The previous storm destroyed two properties and left seven with major damage. Officials warn that driving through flooded neighborhoods can create waves that push water into homes.
cards.body:
Indian River County has extended its local state of emergency through Monday, Nov. 23, as officials prepare for more rain after a storm that destroyed two properties and left seven with major damage. Emergency management officials are urging residents to prepare for possible flooding and avoid driving through flooded neighborhoods, where vehicles can push water into homes.

As of Tuesday, the county also reported 65 properties with minor damage and 97 others affected by the previous storm. Earlier this month, flooding left neighborhoods inundated, roads impassable and traffic disrupted.

Emergency management officials said the ground is saturated, and additional heavy rain could flood areas that did not flood during the last storm. Officials are closely monitoring Heritage Plantation, Whispering Palms and areas near Highland Drive. Crews have been cleaning swales and inspecting drainage systems across the county.

Ryan Lloyd, Deputy Director and Emergency Management Chief for the Indian River County Department of Emergency Services, urged residents countywide to prepare for a possible flood event. He also asked residents to avoid driving into flooded neighborhoods to look at the flooding. “It can create waves that actually go into the houses, and it can make the flooding even worse for residents,” Lloyd said.

The county's emergency information center is open for questions about the flood threat. Residents can call 772-226-4000 for assistance.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie extends boil-water notice for 21,000 customers another 24 hours
hero.body:
A precautionary boil-water notice for about 21,000 customers in western Port St. Lucie has been extended by another 24 hours as the city finishes water-quality testing. Water service has been fully restored, but city officials said the notice will stay in place until laboratory results confirm the water is safe to drink. Sampling is underway following repairs to a damaged water main. Officials said the number of customers affected could keep the advisory in effect beyond the initial 48-hour timeframe. The restoration of service does not mean the boil-water notice has been lifted.

The disruption began when a contractor working on a construction project that was not a city project struck a 36-inch water main near Glades Cut Off Road. Crews finished repairing the main Tuesday evening and began flushing the system. The advisory covers customers in Tradition, Riverland, Western Grove, Wilson Grove, Southern Grove, Copper Creek, Wylder and Verano. It also applies to properties along Glades Cut Off Road. Those areas remain under the precautionary notice while the city completes the testing needed to determine whether the water is safe to drink.

For resident Marcus Rowe, a loss of water pressure was the first indication that something was wrong. “I went to turn on the faucet, and the water pressure was low. I was like, 'what's going on'?” he said. His family has been using bottled water and boiling water to handle daily needs while the advisory remains in place. “Boiling water, doing what they told us to do,” Rowe said. “It's something small, I'm not really sweating it. We're going as far as turning on the water in the fridge so the ice doesn't get accumulated with that tainted water.”

Residents are being advised to keep boiling water used for drinking, cooking, making ice, brushing teeth and washing dishes until the city announces that the notice has ended. Those instructions remain in effect despite the completion of repairs and the return of water service. The additional 24 hours extends the period in which affected customers must continue following the boil-water guidance while awaiting the laboratory findings. City officials said the decision to lift the notice depends on confirmation that the water is safe to drink. For now, the advisory remains in place across the affected western Port St. Lucie communities.

cards.headline: Alexis Cuellar, 24, dies after Port St. Lucie hit-and-run while riding e-scooter
cards.teaser: The driver faces a charge of leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. A former prosecutor says Cuellar’s death could lead to more serious charges.
cards.body:
Alexis Cuellar, 24, of Port St. Lucie, has died after being critically injured in a hit-and-run crash while riding her e-scooter to work Monday, November 16. Cuellar was heading to her job at a nearby Wendy's when she was struck at about 5:10 a.m. in a crosswalk at SW Feather Terrace and SW Gatlin Boulevard.

Police say Tristian Ray Sanchez-Chasmer, 18, of Port St. Lucie, was driving the Chevy Tahoe that hit Cuellar. He had been playing ding-dong-ditch with friends before the crash, according to police. Police say he did not stop to check on Cuellar or render aid. Sanchez-Chasmer was charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury.

Former Palm Beach County State Attorney Dave Aronberg said Sanchez-Chasmer will likely face a more serious charge of leaving the scene of a crash involving death and could also be charged with vehicular homicide. Aronberg said those charges, if filed, would each carry a maximum penalty of 30 years in prison, potentially totaling 60 years if Sanchez-Chasmer is convicted of both.

Aronberg said cases like this require an exhaustive review of the driver's actions, including whether the driver was speeding excessively, running stop signs or driving erratically. He said investigators would examine the vehicle's event data recorder, braking information, marks on the road and the throttle position before impact as part of that review.

hero.headline: Indian River County task force urges residency action for larger homestead exemptions
hero.body:
Indian River County’s Tax Collector and Property Appraiser have formed Task Force 3 to urge residents to establish Florida residency by year’s end to qualify for expanded homestead exemptions. Voters approved Amendment 3 on election day, raising the exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028.

Property Appraiser Wesley Davis and Tax Collector Carole Jean Jordan warned that county offices will close around the upcoming holidays, narrowing the window for residents to obtain Florida identification. Jordan said the push also applies to people already living in Florida who still hold a driver’s license from their previous state. “They can establish residency in an apartment, and then when they buy a home, they can file for homestead.”

Davis emphasized that residents do not need to have a homestead by the end of the year to qualify for the expanded exemption, but they must establish Florida residency by then. Current Florida renters can qualify for the new exemption on a home they buy in the future. New homeowners coming into the state after January 1, 2027 will have to wait five years for the new full exemptions.

The amendment’s impact is already part of discussions about next year’s county budget, both officials acknowledged. Estimates put the county’s potential revenue loss at about $20 million to $30 million over the first couple of years under the amendment. Davis said the change will not end property taxes and will not affect the education portion of tax bills. “About half of everybody's tax bill goes to education, and education is not affected by this at all.”

hero.headline: Indian River County public schools to close Friday as flooding shuts roads
hero.body:
Public schools across Indian River County will be closed Friday, Nov. 20, after flooding left more roads impassable and raised concerns about additional rain. The School District of Indian River County announced the decision Thursday, pointing to localized flooding, already saturated ground and the potential for more heavy rainfall. District officials said the shutdown was intended to protect students, their families and school employees. The announcement applies to all of the county’s public schools. It comes as road closures increase, particularly in Vero Lake Estates, and water levels rise at the district’s North County Transportation compound.

The county’s road closure map showed nine road closures and four lane closures Thursday. Among the roads listed as closed were 100th Court, 103rd Avenue, 104th Avenue, 83rd Street and 87th Street. Those five roads were part of the larger set of closures shown on the map, rather than a complete list of affected roads. Vero Lake Estates was a particular concern in both the district’s closure announcement and the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office’s flooding reports. The district cited the growing number of road closures there, while the sheriff’s office reported additional flooded roads in the neighborhood.

Deputies warned motorists against driving into standing water. Floodwater can be deeper than it looks, and vehicles can stall after entering it, according to the sheriff’s office. That warning accompanied the agency’s reports of more flooded roads in Vero Lake Estates. High-water vehicles are in the area, and anyone who becomes stranded should call 911. The safety message applies even when a driver cannot judge the depth of water covering a road: its appearance may not reflect how deep it actually is. The sheriff’s office’s advice was to stay out of the water rather than attempt to drive through it.

A flood watch remains in effect for Indian River County through Friday evening, with additional showers and thunderstorms possible. The National Weather Service reported that parts of eastern Indian River County had received 2 to 4 inches of rain. The possibility of further rainfall, combined with saturated ground and existing flooding, was among the reasons the district gave for canceling Friday’s classes. Beyond the weather-related closure, schools will also be closed for Thanksgiving break. The district’s immediate concern Thursday was the flooding affecting local roads and its North County Transportation compound, with Friday’s shutdown intended to keep students, families and employees safe.

cards.headline: Flooded roads disrupt Indian River County travel; trash service could be affected
cards.teaser: Officials urged drivers to avoid flooded roads in Vero Lake Estates and watch two potential trouble spots in Fellsmere. Unsafe conditions could also disrupt trash collection and close waste facilities early.
cards.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office reported more flooded roads in Vero Lake Estates on Thursday as heavy rain moved through the county, while county officials warned that unsafe conditions could disrupt trash collection and waste facilities. The sheriff’s office urged drivers to stay off flooded roads because water can be deeper than it appears and can stall vehicles. High-water vehicles are in the area, and anyone who becomes stranded should call 911.

The county’s road closure map listed nine road closures and four lane closures as of 10:53 a.m. Thursday. Roads marked closed included 100th Court, 103rd Avenue, 104th Avenue, 83rd Street and 87th Street. Lane-closure listings included 101st Avenue and West 98th Avenue. In Fellsmere, the city urged drivers to use extreme caution and identified New York Avenue near Hickory Street and North Broadway as potential trouble spots. Those roads could close if rain continues, the city said. City Hall remains open and operating normally.

The county warned that heavy rain and gusty winds could disrupt trash collection. Residents whose streets are flooded were asked not to put their carts in the water. The landfill and customer convenience centers could close early if conditions become unsafe.

A flood watch remains in effect for Indian River County through Friday evening, with more showers and thunderstorms possible. The National Weather Service issued a flood advisory Thursday morning for eastern Indian River and northeastern St. Lucie counties after 2 to 4 inches of rain fell in parts of the area. The advisory warned of minor flooding in low-lying and poorly drained areas. The School District of Indian River County closed all public schools and district offices Thursday, saying saturated ground and expected rain could make travel unsafe for students and staff.

hero.headline: Boil water notice extended 24 hours for 21,000 customers in western Port St. Lucie
hero.body:
A precautionary boil water notice for about 21,000 customers in western Port St. Lucie has been extended by 24 hours as the city continues water-quality testing after a contractor struck a major water main. The contractor was working on a non-city construction project when the 36-inch main was hit near Glades Cut Off Road. Crews finished repairs Tuesday evening and began flushing the water system. Water service has been fully restored, but the precautionary notice remains in place. Customers must continue boiling water for drinking and other specified uses until the city announces that the notice has been lifted.

The affected area includes Tradition, Riverland, Western Grove, Wilson Grove, Southern Grove, Copper Creek, Wylder and Verano. Properties along Glades Cut Off Road are also covered by the advisory. City officials said water-quality sampling is underway and laboratory results must confirm that the water is safe to drink before the notice can end. Officials also said the number of customers affected means the advisory could continue beyond its initial 48-hour timeframe. The 24-hour extension gives the city more time to complete testing, with the notice still dependent on confirmation that the water is safe.

For resident Marcus Rowe, a sudden loss of water pressure was the first indication that something was wrong. “I went to turn on the faucet, and the water pressure was low. I was like, 'what's going on'?” he said. Since the disruption, his family has relied on bottled water and boiled water to meet daily needs. Rowe said the family was following the instructions while taking the inconvenience in stride. “Boiling water, doing what they told us to do,” he said. “It's something small, I'm not really sweating it.” His family is continuing those precautions while the advisory remains active.

Residents covered by the notice are advised to boil water used for drinking, cooking, making ice, brushing their teeth and washing dishes. Those instructions remain in effect despite the restoration of water service and the completion of repairs to the broken main. For households such as the Rowes, that means continuing to use bottled water or boil water for daily needs rather than returning to normal use of tap water. The city has said the notice will stay in place until laboratory testing confirms the water is safe to drink. Customers should continue the precautions until the city announces that the advisory has ended.

cards.headline: Driver arrested in Port St. Lucie hit-and-run that critically injured e-scooter rider
cards.teaser: Tristan Sanchez Chasmer, 18, is being held on a $5,000 bond. Police say he and two passengers had just played a prank at a home about a mile from the crash site.
cards.body:
An 18-year-old driver was arrested in a Port St. Lucie hit-and-run that critically injured a 24-year-old woman riding an e-scooter to work early Monday. Tristan Sanchez Chasmer faces one count of fleeing the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury and is being held on a $5,000 bond.

The crash happened near Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace. Body camera footage shows officers responding to the scene, where the woman was found unconscious in the road. A witness called 911 and helped her before she was airlifted to the hospital. She remains in critical condition.

Port St. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said the driver left without stopping to render aid or contact law enforcement. Detectives identified the vehicle and traced it to Chasmer. According to Niemczyk, Chasmer and two passengers had just ding-dong ditched a home about a mile from the crash site. “He was trying to get away from playing a prank,” Niemczyk said.

Niemczyk said the two passengers exited the truck shortly after the crash, but none of the three called 911. “They're aware that they hit something. I'll say that,” he said. The two passengers are not facing charges.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie police use GTA VI launch to warn against reckless driving
hero.body:
The Port St. Lucie Police Department used Thursday’s Grand Theft Auto VI launch to remind fans that reckless driving and other crimes carry consequences beyond a video game. In a lighthearted safety message, police warned that U.S. 1 and Crosstown are not places to race and that drivers cannot restart after a real-world crash. The department borrowed the game’s wanted-level system to urge residents to avoid attracting police attention. Its reminders included obeying red lights, keeping vehicles off sidewalks and leaving patrol cars alone. Police also joked about avoiding an encounter with the SWAT team, encouraging players to keep the game’s lawbreaking on screen.

Grand Theft Auto VI officially launches Nov. 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. Its fictional state, Leonida, is modeled on Florida, with the Miami-inspired Vice City at its center. The story follows Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos as their criminal plans draw them into a statewide conspiracy. Florida has also become part of the game’s promotion. In September, a large pink sign welcoming visitors to Vice City appeared on Miami’s Kaseya Center under an agreement between Miami-Dade County and Rockstar Games. County officials expected the arrangement to generate nearly $1 million in revenue and provide marketing opportunities. The Miami Heat held a Vice City-themed celebration Wednesday, with a Thursday launch party planned at the Clevelander South Beach and a Rockstar festival scheduled for Saturday.

Other police agencies have used the release to distinguish fictional crimes from real offenses. Atlanta police warned against reckless driving, impaired driving, vehicle theft and violence. In South Florida, law enforcement leaders questioned public involvement in promoting the game. The Miami-Dade Association of Chiefs of Police opposed marketing the county as Vice City, citing depictions of violence against women and police officers. Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz also questioned whether public agencies should promote a game centered on crimes her department works to stop. Port St. Lucie’s message focused on safe driving and keeping virtual criminal behavior away from local roads.

The launch could also disrupt work and viewing habits. A GameSquare survey of 1,000 U.S. employees found that 10% of full-time respondents who identified as gamers planned to miss work on launch day, while another 30% were considering time off. Among those considering an absence, 36% said they would report being sick. Forty-two percent expected lower productivity. Surveyed gamers anticipated spending about $400 on the game and related purchases and playing a median of 15 hours during the opening weekend. Seventy percent said they might skip sports to play, and 42% expected to be less likely to watch NFL games that weekend. Indian River County students had Thursday off because of forecast weather and flooding concerns, while St. Lucie schools reopened.

hero.headline: Flooding leaves Port St. Lucie lanes impassable as crews deploy barricades
hero.body:
Intermittent rain is flooding streets across Port St. Lucie, leaving some lanes impassable and prompting crews to deploy barricades at several locations. Police warn that roadway conditions could change and additional closures may be needed as rain continues.

Standing water is affecting PSL Boulevard at McCorkle Avenue, at Alcantara Boulevard and along the stretch from SW Liberty Drive to Firestone. Barricades are being deployed at each location. Public Works crews are responding to affected areas to place barricades and address water buildup.

On northbound Village Parkway, the outermost lane is impassable south of the fire station. The outermost northbound lane is also impassable south of Discovery Way, where water is beginning to encroach on the second lane. On Tradition Parkway east of Hazel Drive, the outermost lanes in both directions are flooded, and Public Works crews are pumping water from the roadway.

Police are monitoring conditions and urge drivers to use alternate routes around flooded areas. Drivers should not drive through standing or moving water, go around barricades or enter closed roads.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie homeowner says rain is worsening unrepaired Hurricane Milton damage
cards.teaser: Caryn McGregor says water is entering through her ceiling, windows and vents as she awaits Rebuild Florida assistance. A repair assessment documents unrepaired storm damage and proposed work inside her home.
cards.body:
Recent heavy rain is worsening unrepaired Hurricane Milton damage at Caryn McGregor's Port St. Lucie home, she said. She is awaiting assistance through the state's Rebuild Florida Housing Repair and Replacement Program, which provides housing repairs or replacement.

Water continues to enter through the ceiling, windows and vents, with rainwater observed dripping inside the house. McGregor is using buckets and towels while she waits for permanent repairs. “I'm scared my ceiling's gonna come down,” she said.

A repair assessment lists Oct. 9, 2024, as the date of loss and Jan. 6, 2026, as the date her home was inspected. It documents unrepaired storm damage and says McGregor reported plumbing problems since the hurricane. The proposed work includes repairs involving ceilings, walls, plumbing, siding, appliances, drywall and doors.

McGregor said her roof was damaged when Hurricane Milton struck Florida in October 2024. She initially contacted her insurance company but could not afford the deductible, she said. She later sought help through Rebuild Florida and said the repairs remain unfinished after the January inspection.

McGregor said she has been told the project is waiting on permits before work can proceed. The assessment documents the damage identified during the inspection and the proposed repairs.

The continued water intrusion has left McGregor worried about water, mold and the ceiling collapsing. “I can't even have my son living here because the ceiling, I'm scared of it falling on him and hurting him,” she said. She also said water has damaged her washer, dryer and dishwasher.

“I want them to help us fix our house,” McGregor said. “They said they were going to.”

hero.headline: Martin County sheriff readies high-water vehicles in Stuart and Indiantown
hero.body:
The Martin County Sheriff’s Office is preparing high-water rescue vehicles in Stuart and Indiantown for expected heavy rain and potential flooding, with a team on standby for urgent calls from the emergency operations center.

Two high-water vehicles are at the sheriff’s office in Stuart, and another is stationed in Indiantown in case that area floods. The preparations are part of Martin County officials’ response to expected heavy rainfall across the Treasure Coast.

Sheriff John Budensiek describes the retired military vehicles, known as MTVs, as the agency’s worst-case-scenario vehicles for natural disasters such as hurricanes and flash flooding. They sit high off the ground and are heavy enough to drive through hurricane-force winds and high water.

“Hopefully we don't need them. But we're in a position where if we get the rains that are expected and if we get the flooding that we've had here in the last couple of weeks, again, we're prepared to try to help our citizens as best we can,” Budensiek said.

hero.headline: Woman, 24, dies after Port St. Lucie scooter hit-and-run; enhanced charges expected
hero.body:
A 24-year-old woman has died from injuries suffered in a hit-and-run crash while riding an electric scooter in Port St. Lucie, police said Wednesday. Following her death, police said they anticipate the State Attorney’s Office will pursue enhanced or additional charges based on the circumstances and the outcome of the investigation.

Investigators identified the alleged driver as 18-year-old Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer. He was arrested and charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, a second-degree felony, police said. The expectation of enhanced or additional charges follows the woman’s death at approximately 9:23 p.m. Tuesday.

The crash happened around 5:10 a.m. Monday near the intersection of Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace. Police said a vehicle struck the woman as she rode an electric scooter. Investigators allege the driver left without stopping to help her or notify law enforcement.

The department’s Traffic Homicide Investigations Unit identified the vehicle as a gray Chevrolet Tahoe and located it at a Port St. Lucie home, according to police. Investigators said Sanchez-Chasmer had been playing “ding dong ditch” with friends shortly before the crash. According to police, the group was leaving a home where they had been participating in the prank when the vehicle struck the woman.

hero.headline: Indian River County public schools, district offices closed Thursday over flood risk
hero.body:
All School District of Indian River County public schools and district offices will be closed Thursday, Nov. 19, because saturated ground and expected heavy rain could make travel unsafe for students and employees, district officials announced Wednesday. The district cited potential flooding and concerns about travel to and from schools in its decision to cancel classes and close offices.

“With ground conditions already saturated, we cannot be confident that students and staff will be able to travel safely to and from school,” the district said. “Weather conditions may also affect staff members' ability to report to work.” The closure comes about two weeks after prolonged rainfall caused significant flooding in Indian River County.

A flood watch for Indian River County remains in effect through Friday evening as another round of rain moves through the Treasure Coast. The National Weather Service forecast calls for a 95% chance of precipitation Thursday, with about 1.74 inches of rain possible. The National Weather Service is also reporting a high surf advisory and rip current statement for the area.

Indian River County officials have warned residents that roads not officially listed as closed could still have standing water or other hazards. Drivers should obey barricades and never attempt to drive through floodwater. District officials said they will continue monitoring conditions and release additional information through official district communication channels.
